meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be sincere; be brief; be seated'?
meta.ogDescription: Not FDR's coinage. Quote Investigator traces this speech advice to 1935 stage actors; FDR's son James credited his father in 1940.

answer.label: Not Franklin D. Roosevelt — anonymous, circulating by 1935
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ found the advice in use in 1935: the actor Richard ‘Skeets’ Gallagher credited his mother, William ‘Buster’ Collier Jr. credited his father, and a Wisconsin toastmaster used it too. QI says the creator is anonymous. FDR’s name first appears in January 1940, when his son James told a Hollywood audience that his father had given him these “hints on speechmaking.” Roosevelt may have repeated the line, but he almost certainly did not coin it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Journal-Every Evening (Wilmington, Delaware), February 16, 1935, p. 19. Skeets Gallagher credits his mother
The Washington Post, January 13, 1940, p. 8. James Roosevelt credits his father
“Be sincere; be brief; be seated.” In Bill Adler, Presidential Wit from Washington to Johnson (1966), p. 165, per QI
Anonymous. FDR is unlikely to have coined it

source.excerpt: The other day James Roosevelt opened a talk he made at Hollywood by saying: “My father gave me these hints on speechmaking. Be sincere … be brief … be seated.”
trail: 1880: a precursor. Dr. C. Z. Weiser closes a Franklin and Marshall College commencement speech with “Stand up, speak up and then shut up” (The Weekly New Era, Lancaster, per Quote Investigator ↗).

1935: Skeets Gallagher (February) credits his mother: “always be brief, sincere and be seated.” Buster Collier Jr. (March, The Hollywood Reporter) credits his father: “Be sincere . . . be brief . . . be seated!” QI reads these close-together, unrelated uses as a sign of anonymous origin (QI ↗).
1940: James Roosevelt credits his father in Hollywood. The Washington Post reports it in January, and Reader’s Digest reprints it in June (QI ↗).

Later: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among FDR’s quotes under “Posthumous publications.” Its only source is a secondhand citation to Paul L. Soper’s Basic Public Speaking (1963), p. 12, describing it as advice to his son James.
source.excerptNote: The earliest tie to FDR, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. This is the son reporting his father’s advice, not Roosevelt’s own words in any speech or letter. The same article called the saying a variant of the old advice to “stand up . . . speak up . . . shut up.”

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: About Anonymous
author.metaLine: Unknown originator · American speechmaking advice in circulation by 1935
author.bio: The three-part rule for speakers has no known author. Quote Investigator found it in 1935, credited by stage and screen performers to their own parents, and treats it as a descendant of the older “Stand up, speak up and then shut up” (recorded in 1880). Franklin D. Roosevelt became attached to it in 1940 through his son James, and a 1966 presidential joke book printed the semicolon wording as his advice to James.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This tidy piece of speaking advice has been credited to a president, to two actors’ parents and to “Dad.” Every one of those credits is secondhand.

items.why: The only period evidence is his son James telling a Hollywood audience in January 1940 that “My father gave me these hints on speechmaking.” QI calls this “some evidence” that FDR used the expression, but notes it “was already circulating before 1940” and that “it is unlikely that F.D.R. coined it” (Quote Investigator ↗).

Gallagher said his mother had often told him to “always be brief, sincere and be seated.” QI says she could conceivably have coined it, but other unrelated 1935 uses suggest the creator “remains anonymous” (QI ↗).

Buster Collier Jr. told a Broadway gathering “My father gave me these hints on speech-making,” the same framing James Roosevelt used five years later. In December 1940 Hedda Hopper ascribed the saying to Collier (QI ↗).
H. Jackson Brown Jr.’s A Father’s Book of Wisdom prints it as “How To Make A Speech: Be Sincere Be Brief Be Seated — Dad,” which shows how naturally the line passes as parental advice (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the advice is anonymous and was in circulation by 1935. FDR’s son credited him with it in 1940, which tied his name to it, but FDR almost certainly did not originate it (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the Roosevelt name stuck
lead: The saying is a three-beat formula held together by the repeated “be.” QI points out that it echoes an older three-beat rule held together by “up”: “Stand up, speak up and then shut up,” recorded in Pennsylvania in 1880 and in England in 1896. The 1940 Washington Post item that first tied the line to FDR itself called it a variant of that old advice.

What carried the Roosevelt version was the messenger. A sitting president’s son repeated it in Hollywood, and Reader’s Digest reprinted it within months. By 1966 a presidential joke book printed it as “FDR’s advice to his son James,” in the semicolon form most people quote today.
context.pull: “My father gave me these hints on speechmaking.” Two different sons said this, five years apart.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI: the earliest FDR ascription is The Washington Post, January 13, 1940, p. 8, where James Roosevelt says "My father gave me these hints on speechmaking. Be sincere … be brief … be seated." QI calls it unlikely FDR coined it.

QI: the earliest evidence is February 1935 (Skeets Gallagher, crediting his mother, Journal-Every Evening p. 19), followed by Buster Collier Jr. in March 1935 and Rev. Delbert Basche in June 1935. QI concludes the creator is anonymous.

QI: the 1880 precursor "Stand up, speak up and then shut up" (C. Z. Weiser), Reader's Digest June 1940, Hedda Hopper December 1940, Esar 1943, Adler 1966 p. 165 ("Be sincere; be brief; be seated.") and H. Jackson Brown Jr. 1988. Posted October 1, 2023; updated May 12, 2024.
Wikiquote's FDR page lists "Be sincere, be brief, be seated." under Quotes > Posthumous publications as advice to his son James, citing Paul L. Soper, Basic Public Speaking (1963), p. 12.
James Roosevelt was the eldest son of Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Richard "Skeets" Gallagher was an American actor (1891–1955).
William Collier Jr. was an American stage and film actor (1902–1987).
